post.caption: Poudretteite is named for a quarry family. The Poudrette family owned and ran a quarry in Quebec. Seven tiny crystals turned up there in the mid 1960s. Each was only a few millimeters across and nearly colorless. It was not recognized as a new mineral until 1986. Until 2000, those Quebec crystals were the only known poudretteite. That year, a stone from Mogok in Myanmar proved to be one. It weighed about three carats and glowed purple pink. Poudretteite is about 5 on the Mohs scale, where diamond is 10. The Smithsonian holds one among the largest ever cut, at 9.41 carats.
